system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2151-12-01 20:32:00 to 2151-12-03 15:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, kidney transplant, peripheral vascular disease, and prior amputations was admitted for worsening foot wounds on the right heel, lateral foot, and site of prior great toe amputation, with purulent drainage and foul odor. He had been unable to secure an outpatient vascular surgery appointment. Blood pressure was severely elevated on arrival, attributed to missed medications. Imaging showed soft tissue swelling without evidence of osteomyelitis. He was treated with IV antibiotics initially, then transitioned to oral Bactrim. Vascular and podiatry teams recommended medical management with betadine dressings and outpatient vascular studies. His hypertension improved with reinitiation of home medications, and transplant function remained stable. He was discharged home with follow-up plans and instructions for wound care and medication adherence.
problems: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with foot ulcer
Non-pressure chronic ulcer of right heel and midfoot with unspecified severity
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic peripheral angiopathy without gangrene

Abd:  Soft, NT/ND, scarring consistent with stated PSH
Ext:  LUE s/p HD graft.  RUE s/p partial amputations of R ___ 
and

wound on medial heel is smaller still.  No gross purulence is

No left groin hematoma

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ was admitted on ___ for hydration prior to his 
procedure. Nephrology was consulted to aid on his management 
given his renal disease. On ___, he underwent balloon 
angioplasty of the right anterior tibial artery, first with a 2 
mm balloon and followed by a 2.5 mm balloon. Nine cc of 
visipaque were used and his right DP, which was previously 
absent, was palpable. For details on the procedure, please refer

Discharge Instructions:
Mr. ___, 

You were admitted to the ___ 
for management of your peripheral artery disease and associated 
non-healing ulcer of the right foot. You underwent balloon 
angioplasty of the right anterior tibial artery. The minimal 
necessary amount of contrast was used in order to protect your 
kidney function. The procedure went well. The Nephrology team 
participated in your care. Your renal function today is stable. 
You have recovered well and are ready to return home to continue 
your recovery. Please see the following instructions regarding 
your discharge. 

MEDICATIONS:
 Take clopidogrel 75 mg daily for one month.
 Take Aspirin 81mg (enteric coated) once daily. 
 Do not stop Aspirin unless your Vascular Surgeon instructs you 
to do so. 
 Hold Chlorthalidone until you see your Nephrologist next week. 
Continue all other medications you were taking before surgery.
 You make take acetaminophen for pain or discomfort

WHAT TO EXPECT AT HOME:
It is normal to have slight swelling of the legs:
 Elevate your leg above the level of your heart (use ___ 
pillows or a recliner) every ___ hours throughout the day and at 
night
 Avoid prolonged periods of standing or sitting without your 
legs elevated

ACTIVITIES:
 When you go home, you may walk and go up and down stairs
 You may shower (let the soapy water run over groin incision, 
rinse and pat dry)
 Your incision may be left uncovered, unless you have small 
amounts of drainage from the wound, then place a dry dressing or 
band aid over the area that is draining, as needed
 No heavy lifting, pushing or pulling (greater than 5 lbs) for 
1 week (to allow groin puncture to heal)
 After 1 week, you may resume sexual activity
 After 1 week, gradually increase your activities and distance 
walked as you can tolerate
 No driving until you are no longer taking pain medications

CALL THE OFFICE FOR: ___
 Numbness, coldness or pain in lower extremities 
 Temperature greater than 101.5F for 24 hours
 New or increased drainage from incision or white, yellow or 
green drainage from incisions
 Bleeding from groin puncture site

FOR SUDDEN, SEVERE BLEEDING OR SWELLING (Groin puncture site or 
incision)
 Lie down, keep leg straight and have someone apply firm 
pressure to area for 10 minutes. If bleeding stops, call 
vascular office. If bleeding does not stop, call ___ for 
transfer to closest Emergency Room. 

Good Luck!
 
Followup Instructions:
___

procedures.long_title: Dilation of Right Anterior Tibial Artery, Open Approach

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of the surgical team members. We’ve admitted you tonight to prepare for a procedure tomorrow to help improve blood flow to your right foot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. The ulcers on my foot have been getting worse, and it’s been hard to walk. I’m glad we’re doing something about the circulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history of diabetes and peripheral artery disease has made it harder for wounds to heal. We’re planning an angioplasty tomorrow to open up the artery in your leg and help your foot get better blood supply.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this done before, right? On the same leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve had prior angioplasty and stenting. This time, we’re focusing on the anterior tibial artery, which has narrowed again. We’ll use a small balloon to open it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they use contrast dye? I remember last time my kidney function was a concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’ll use the minimal amount of contrast needed, and we’re also using CO2 to help reduce the risk to your kidneys. Nephrology is involved to make sure we protect your transplant function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve been taking all my meds, but my blood sugars are still high. A1c was 10.6 last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know diabetes makes healing harder. You’re on insulin, and we’ll keep that going. The goal is to stabilize everything so your foot can heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ulcers? They’re not infected now, are they?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of active infection—no fever, redness, or pus. But they’re not healing due to poor blood flow. That’s why the procedure is so important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my blood pressure? I noticed my chlorthalidone wasn’t on the list today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nephrology recommended holding the chlorthalidone for now because of your kidney transplant. We’ll restart it after your follow-up next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. So no water pill until I see them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re monitoring your kidney function closely. Your creatinine is stable at 1.4, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day for your procedure. You’ll go to the angiography suite around noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under light sedation. The team will access the artery in your left groin and guide the catheter to your right leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Left side for access, right side for treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. It’s safer and easier to work from the opposite side. The procedure should take about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The angioplasty went well. We opened the right anterior tibial artery with a 2 mm and then a 2.5 mm balloon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it work? Did the blood flow improve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Before, your dorsalis pedis pulse was absent. Now it’s palpable. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Any complications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. We used only 9 cc of contrast, and your left groin site is clean with no hematoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidney? That’s what I worry about most.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your renal function remains stable. Creatinine is still 1.4. Nephrology is satisfied with how things went.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about meds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll start clopidogrel today—a blood thinner to keep the artery open. You’ll take it for 30 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like Plavix? I’ve taken that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, clopidogrel is Plavix. You’ll also keep taking aspirin. Don’t stop either without talking to vascular surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Can I walk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can walk, but avoid heavy lifting—nothing over 5 pounds—for a week to let the groin site heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No lifting. Got it. And driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off on driving until you’re off the pain meds. Once you’re not taking oxycodone, you can resume.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable, you’re eating and walking, and your foot looks unchanged—no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll discharge you. Keep elevating your leg to reduce swelling, and follow the wound care instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when do I see the doctors again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nephrology within a week, vascular surgery in a month. Call if you have fever, new pain, bleeding from the groin, or changes in your foot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your insulin and medications, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can shower. Let the water run over the groin site, then pat it dry. No need to cover it unless there’s drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the foot ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep doing the betadine dressings as before. The improved blood flow should help them heal over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and call us if anything changes. You’re cleared to go home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, kidney transplant, and peripheral artery disease was admitted for management of non-healing ulcers on his right foot. He underwent balloon angioplasty of the right anterior tibial artery to improve blood flow, which was successful as evidenced by the return of a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse. The procedure used minimal contrast to protect kidney function, and his renal values remained stable. He was started on clopidogrel for 30 days and advised to hold chlorthalidone until nephrology follow-up. He recovered well, with stable vital signs and pain control, and was discharged home with instructions for wound care, activity restrictions, and follow-up appointments with nephrology and vascular surgery.
